description: Our team is developing an interactive, web-based Martian map and survival guide to assist future explorers.
summary:
RedMap is an interactive Martian mapping and mission-planning platform developed to address NASA’s “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge. It brings diverse NASA and USGS datasets together in one unified interface, helping future astronauts explore Mars and make informed decisions.

The platform features interactive 3D and high-resolution 2D maps, integrating terrain, elevation, spectral layers, geological landmarks, and detailed surface imagery. Its intelligent A* pathfinding engine analyzes terrain conditions to identify safer routes while considering slopes, crater rims, and other hazards. RedMap also introduces physics-based astronaut EVA and rover simulations, estimating spacesuit life-support consumption, rover driving limits, and mission duration. Additionally, NASA space-weather alerts and radiation measurements support automated GO, CAUTION, and NO-GO assessments.

RedMap addresses the challenge by transforming complex planetary data into practical, location-specific information for exploration and survival. This is important because future astronauts cannot always depend on real-time communication with Earth. By combining mapping, route planning, environmental awareness, and mission simulations, RedMap aims to make Martian exploration safer, smarter, and more self-reliant.
details:
RedMap: An Interplanetary Survival Guide for Mars

How We Addressed the Challenge

NASA’s challenge, “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map,” asks a critical question: How can we turn decades of Martian satellite data into a practical survival map for future astronauts?

On Mars, a straight line between two points can easily lead an astronaut over a deadly crater cliff, drain a rover’s battery before it can return, or leave a crew exposed during a solar storm.

Team Red Matter built RedMap to solve this problem. Instead of just showing pretty pictures of Mars, RedMap turns real NASA orbital maps, laser elevation data, live space weather, and rover surface photos into a complete EVA (Extravehicular Activity) Mission & Survival Planner.

RedMap connects three workspaces, centered around our flagship EVA Route Planner:

  1. Explainable EVA Route Planner (/route — Core Feature): A tactical crater map (25 cm/px detail) paired with a smart pathfinder that plans Fastest, Safest, and Most Scientific routes, simulates astronaut spacesuit & rover survival limits, finds nearby natural radiation shelters, and includes a 360° Helmet Visor View with real NASA rover panoramas.
  2. 3D/2D Planetary Atlas (/): A true-to-scale 3D Mars globe and 2D global map with 6 switchable NASA science layers, 430+ searchable landmarks, and 13 historic/active NASA mission hubs.
  3. Martian Survival Guide (/guide): A live astronaut field manual with a real-time Mars clock (MTC), Earth–Mars radio delay calculator, and clear safety rules.

How RedMap Works?

1. Core Feature: Explainable EVA Route Planner

The Route Planner is the heart of RedMap. It helps astronauts plan a safe, scientifically valuable walk or rover drive inside two of Mars’s most important exploration zones: Gale Crater (Curiosity’s home) and Jezero Crater (Perseverance’s home).

A. Ultra-Detailed Crater Map & Custom Route Pinning

  • Zoom Down to Boulders (25 cm/px): Using OpenSeadragon, astronauts can smoothly zoom from regional CTX imagery (5 m/px) all the way down to MRO HiRISE orthomosaics (25 cm/px) to inspect individual rock outcrops, ancient riverbeds, and steep scarps.
  • Click-to-Plan & Custom Detours: Users can choose famous preset locations (like Gediz Vallis → Boxwork Ridge in Gale, or Octavia E. Butler Landing → Neretva Vallis in Jezero), swap start and end points in one click, or tap anywhere on the map to set custom Start/Destination pins and add up to 4 custom Detour Stops (D1–D4).
    • Slope Risk (steep walls and cliffs)
    • Low Ground (deep pits and enclosed crater bowls)
    • No-Go Zones (impassable terrain and safety buffer zones)

B. Smart Controls & Three Route Strategies (Fastest, Safest, Most Scientific)

Before planning, astronauts can customize their mission limits inside Route & Suit Constraints:

  • Max Slope Limit (5°–30°)
  • Daily EVA Hours per Sol (2–10 hours)
  • Equipment & Sample Load (0–30 kg) — automatically shows how heavy that gear feels in Mars’s 0.38g gravity
  • Science Stop Suggestions (on/off)

RedMap then calculates and compares three route options side by side inside a background Web Worker (so the screen never freezes):

  1. Fastest Route: Finds the shortest practical path while still staying under safe risk limits (Risk ≤ 40, no critical dangers).
  2. Safest Route: Actively avoids steep hills, bumpy boulder fields, side-slopes, and deep craters—using smart optimization so it doesn't make pointless detours.
  3. Most Scientific Route: Gently bends the path toward high-value geological outcrops (clay, water channels, boxwork ridges) without putting the crew in danger.

C. Real NASA Elevation Calibration & "Why This Route?" Explanations

  • Self-Calibrating NASA Terrain: RedMap reads real NASA MGS MOLA (463 m/px) elevation tiles right in the browser, calibrates them against 12 known NASA landing sites (R² ≥ 0.85), smooths out blocky pixel steps (de-terracing) for short crater walks, and adds surveyed HiRISE canyon/delta landforms. If a remote tile fails to load, RedMap switches to a backup terrain model and honestly tells the user whether the route used real NASA elevation or backup terrain.
  • Plain-English Route Reasoning (Why This Route?): Instead of just drawing a mysterious line, RedMap compares the planned path against a straight line and explains every choice clearly—for example, how much steep slope it avoided, how much climbing it saved, and why each numbered waypoint turned (MOLA, CRISM, HiRISE, or CREW reasons).

D. Astronaut Life-Support (PLSS), Rover Physics & GO / CAUTION / NO-GO Verdict

Every route is stress-tested against real Martian survival physics:

  • Spacesuit Life-Support (xEMU PLSS): Tracks single-sol Oxygen (0.76 kg), Cooling Water (3.60 L), and Suit Battery (620 Wh). Climbing steep slopes, carrying heavy rock samples (0–30 kg), and freezing below -65°C drain supplies faster. RedMap always enforces a 2-hour emergency walk-back reserve and a 30-minute daylight safety buffer before sunset.
  • 2-Crew Pressurized Rover Physics: Models a 1,200 kg rover driving across loose Martian dust (g = 3.71 m/s², Crr = 0.15), including 30% downhill regenerative braking, 300 W cabin power, a 15 kWh battery (25% emergency reserve), flat safe rest stops, and the exact Point-of-No-Return (pnrKm)—the point beyond which the rover cannot make it back on remaining battery.
  • 9-Point Autonomous Flight Verdict (GO / CAUTION / NO-GO): Instantly grades the entire mission across 9 safety checks (slope limits, whether every leg is safe to walk back ≤ 12°, suit supplies, rover power, sunset margin, dust season, radiation, and radio delay) and lists kilometer-by-kilometer warnings (km X–Y).
  • Sol-by-Sol EVA Timeline: Breaks multi-day traverses into daily schedules showing distance, work hours, and rest/recharge stops per Martian sol.

E. Live NASA Space Weather & Nearest Natural Radiation Shelter

Mars has no global magnetic field to block space radiation. RedMap solves this in real time:

  • Live NASA DONKI Alerts: Connects to NASA’s live DONKI space weather feed (Solar Energetic Particles & CMEs over the past 14 days) and combines it with Curiosity’s MSL RAD surface radiation baseline (0.64 mSv/sol normal, up to 4.80 mSv/sol during severe solar storms).
  • Automatic Shelter Finder: RedMap scans the MOLA elevation grid along the route to pinpoint the Nearest Natural Radiation Shelter—such as a steep crater wall, ridge, or canyon alcove that physically blocks 18%–46%+ of the open sky—and tells the crew the exact distance, direction, and time (Shelter ETA) to reach cover if an alarm goes off.

F. Interactive Traverse Simulation, Science Corridor & 360° Helmet Visor HUD

  • Elevation Profile & Live Traverse Preview: Users can scrub their mouse across the Elevation Profile chart or hit Play (1× / 2× speed) to watch the rover/astronaut travel along the HiRISE map while O₂, cooling water, battery, Point-of-No-Return alerts, and Shelter ETA update live at every meter.
  • Science Corridor Explorer (±1–30 km): Use the lateral corridor slider and category filters (Boxwork, Water, Minerals, Geology, Atmosphere) to inspect 16 catalogued astrobiology & geology sites, see exact round-trip detour km, click "Center on Map", or check them to add them directly to your route.
  • 360° Surface Reconnaissance & Spacesuit Helmet Visor HUD: Click any recon station along the route to open 23+ real NASA/JPL 360° surface panoramas (from Perseverance, Curiosity, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking, Pathfinder, Phoenix, and InSight). Inside the viewer, astronauts can click glowing geological hotspots (showing mineral notes, ground footing hazards, and sampling tools) and toggle the Spacesuit Helmet Visor HUD—featuring a scrolling 360° compass, live O₂/H₂O/Battery bars synced to the simulation, metabolic rate (kcal/h), Earth delay, and a 1-click "Jump to Shelter" button.
  • One-Click Mission Card Export: Export the complete route plan, coordinates, life-support budget, warnings, and abort shelters as a printable .txt Mission Card or .json data file.

2. Interactive 3D/2D Planetary Atlas

To help crews pick landing regions and understand global context before zooming into a crater, RedMap includes a full planetary atlas powered by CesiumJS built specifically on Mars’s real shape (Cesium.Ellipsoid.MARS, radius 3,389.5 km):

  • 6 Switchable NASA Mars Trek Layers: Toggle instantly between Terrain (Viking MDIM 2.1), Elevation (MOLA + HRSC Color Shaded Relief), Geological Features, Minerals (TES Sheet Silicates & Glass), Thermal IR / Temperature (Odyssey THEMIS Daytime IR dynamically colorized in-browser via a 256-color thermal lookup table), and Atmosphere (TES Atmospheric Dust).
  • Smart Search & Clutter-Free Labels: Morph between the 3D Globe (with realistic Martian orange-red atmosphere and day/night terminator) and a 2D Map, search 430+ IAU-named Mars landmarks, and rely on altitude-aware anti-collision labels.
  • 13 NASA Mission Hubs: Toggle NASA Missions Mode to fly to Perseverance, Curiosity, Opportunity, Spirit, Pathfinder, InSight, Phoenix, Viking 1/2, MRO, Odyssey, MGS, and MAVEN with mission facts, instruments, and real surface photos.

3. Martian Interplanetary Survival Guide

Complementing the Route Planner, RedMap’s Survival Guide serves as an always-on astronaut reference manual featuring:

  • Live Mars Telemetry Strip (updates every second):
    • Coordinated Mars Time (MTC) and Mars Sol Date (MSD) (24h 39m 35s Martian sol)
    • Solar Longitude (Ls) showing whether Mars is currently in Perihelion Global Dust Season (Ls 180°–330°)
    • Live Earth–Mars Light Delay (6.2–44.6 min round-trip radio lag based on orbital distance)
    • Gale & Jezero Daylight Windows (exact sunrise to sunset in Local True Solar Time)
  • 4 Filterable Survival Protocol Sections: Clear visual cards explaining PLSS & Rover Dynamics, Radiation & Sky-Dome Shielding, Cryogenic Cold (-90°C) & Dust Hazards, and Autonomous Light-Delay Operations.

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Turns Complex Space Maps into Clear Survival Decisions: Converts raw orbital images into answers astronauts actually need—Can my suit oxygen last? Will the rover make it back? Where is the closest storm shelter?
  • Explains Every Choice in Plain Language: Instead of giving a black-box route, RedMap shows why a detour is safer than a straight line.
  • Runs Anywhere in a Browser: Zero expensive GIS software or backend servers needed—plus built-in offline fallbacks (local globe textures, SVG horizons, and backup terrain) keep the app working smoothly even on unstable connections.

What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  • Astronaut Autonomy Under Radio Blackouts: With Earth–Mars round-trip radio delays up to 44.6 minutes, crews cannot wait for Mission Control to steer them around a cliff or solar storm. RedMap demonstrates how onboard software can make fast, life-saving decisions locally.
  • Inspiring STEM & Planetary Exploration: Lets students, educators, and citizen explorers interactively test real rover terrains in Gale and Jezero Craters and see Mars through the eyes of actual NASA landers.
  • Open-Source Mission Toolkit: Offers a clean, unit-tested codebase (a-azme/redmap) that researchers and developers can extend for future lunar or Martian traverse simulations.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES Modules / JSX), HTML5, CSS3
  • Frontend & State: React 19.2, React Router DOM 7.18, Vite 8.3, Tailwind CSS 4.3, Zustand 5.0, Lucide React
  • Mapping & Graphics: OpenSeadragon 6.1 (25 cm/px crater deep-zoom), CesiumJS 1.146 (Cesium.Ellipsoid.MARS 3D/2D globe), HTML5 Canvas 2D (thermal LUT shader & MOLA pixel calibration), SVG (elevation profiles & Visor HUD)
  • Algorithms & Physics: Web Workers (routeWorker.js), MinHeap A* + Elastic Path Smoothing, Linear Regression (R² MOLA calibration), Binary-Search Route Optimization, Newtonian Rover & xEMU PLSS Physics, Allison & McEwen Mars24 Timekeeping, Keplerian Light-Delay Ephemeris
  • Testing & Hosting: Node.js Test Runner (node --test across 6 unit test suites), ESLint 10, Git/GitHub, Vercel

How Is Our Project Creative?

  • Automatic NASA Elevation Calibration in the Browser: Instead of hardcoding fake heights or relying on a heavy backend server, RedMap reads raw NASA MOLA image tiles in a hidden canvas, calibrates them against 12 real NASA landing sites using linear regression, and smooths out pixel steps for hyperlocal crater walks.
  • Everything Synced to One Timeline: Dragging your finger along the Elevation Profile—or clicking Preview Traverse—moves the rover on the 25 cm/px HiRISE map, updates suit O₂/H₂O/battery, flags Point-of-No-Return, and syncs live with the 360° Helmet Visor HUD inside real NASA rover photos.
  • Real-Time Client-Side Thermal Coloring: Converts grayscale Odyssey THEMIS infrared tiles into a smooth false-color temperature map directly in the browser using a 256-entry color lookup table.
  • Safety-First Binary-Search Blending: Even when a user picks Fastest or Most Scientific, RedMap automatically balances the route so it never crosses critical danger thresholds.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Long Earth–Mars Radio Delays (6.2–44.6 min): Built the entire GO/CAUTION/NO-GO verdict, Point-of-No-Return check, and Radiation Shelter finder to work autonomously without waiting for Earth.
  • Mars’s 0.38g Gravity & Loose Dust: Modeled lower gravity, carrying up to 30 kg of rock samples, high rolling resistance (Crr = 0.15), downhill energy recovery, and steep slopes (> 12°) that a crew cannot safely climb back out of.
  • Extreme Cold & Global Dust Storms: Enforced a 30-minute pre-sunset buffer against -90°C nights, extra battery draw for suit heaters below -65°C, and dust storm warnings (Ls 180°–330°).
  • Solar Particle Storms: Paired live NASA DONKI alerts with terrain-based sky shielding (18%–46%+) so astronauts always know the fastest path to natural cover.
  • Smooth Performance & Honesty: Offloaded heavy pathfinding to Web Workers, protected WebGL memory across page switches, and clearly labeled real NASA DEM data vs. fallback terrain.

  • Use of AI: AI tools, including Claude, ChatGPT, and Google Gemini, were used during development for brainstorming, debugging, and code review. These tools assisted the development process but did not replace the application's core computational logic. All planetary physics, timekeeping, and pathfinding calculations run deterministically within the application and are verified through automated unit tests.
  • Disclaimer: RedMap is an educational and simulation-grade exploration tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge and is not certified for real aerospace flight operations.
